title: Probe asyncRewake: headless runs and more than 8 Signal wakes
domain: complex: what Claude Code 2.1.311 does shows only by running it; its binary reads CLAUDE_CODE_STOP_HOOK_BLOCK_CAP ?? 8 and backgrounds asyncRewake only when the session is interactive or has streaming input, which suggests but does not prove both risks

score_evidence.value: decides whether Signal conversations can stall (G-2 target: 0 stuck sessions) and whether a user-scope install holds the owner's claude -p runs
score_evidence.time: must finish before install-guards and publish-v1 (G-1 due 2026-11-05); the owner's other projects run claude -p in screen sessions
score_evidence.risk: the riskiest unknown in the queue; one run settles both questions and decides what install-guards detects
score_evidence.size: two throwaway hooks in a new scratch folder, about an hour

promise: A run, not a change. In a new scratch folder (not this repo, whose untracked .claude/settings.local.json carries the owner's live relay hooks), with throwaway hooks, measure on Claude Code 2.1.311 and record with wuwei plan run: (1) whether claude -p waits for a Stop hook marked asyncRewake; (2) how many consecutive asyncRewake wakes (exit 2) an interactive session takes with no typed prompt, past 8; (3) what the woken turns' Stop input and the hook environment carry (stop_hook_active, and the variable that marks a print-mode run, such as CLAUDE_CODE_ENTRYPOINT), so install-guards can tell a headless run apart. Outside: any change to signal_cc. If wakes stop at 8 or fewer, file the follow-up before closing.
acceptance: Given a scratch folder whose .claude/settings.local.json holds a Stop hook with asyncRewake true that sleeps 20 s and then writes a marker file, when claude -p 'reply ok' runs there, then the record states the wall time and whether the run waited for the hook.

Given an interactive claude session in a detached screen with an asyncRewake Stop hook that exits 2 with 'reply with the next number' up to 12 times and logs each call, when one typed prompt starts it and nobody types again, then the record states how many wakes happened and whether the 9th to 12th did.

Given both hooks log their stdin and the names of their environment variables, when they run in print mode and in interactive mode, then the record lists stop_hook_active for each call and the variable that tells the two modes apart, with no secret values copied.
Given wakes stop at or before the 9th, when the run is recorded, then a follow-up item names the cap and a mitigation (for example a Signal notice that the session needs a prompt typed at the Mac).
why: Riskiest unknown first: the binary suggests claude -p runs this Stop hook synchronously (up to 300 s at the Mac, 3600 s away) and that wakes may cap at 8; one hour of probing decides install-guards.

title: A fresh install does no harm: no Stop listener in headless runs, silent where it cannot run

title: Away switch: tell the relay from Signal that you are away or back
domain: complicated: two desk commands and a presence override through the existing Presence port; it changes the default where idle time is unknown

score_evidence.value: one of G-2's four named follow-ups; gives non-macOS users a workable default once G-1 makes the plugin public
score_evidence.time: G-2 due 2026-11-19; leave-digest needs its definition of leaving
score_evidence.risk: retires the README limit 'Idle detection is macOS only. Elsewhere every prompt goes to Signal first'
score_evidence.size: two commands, a flag file, a presence rule, tests

promise: The owner can say from Signal that they are away or back, and the relay follows that over the idle timer. A plain 'away' turns the switch on: prompts go to Signal whatever the idle time, and Mac input does not hand them back. A plain 'back', or a prompt typed at the Mac (UserPromptSubmit), turns it off. 'status' shows whether it is on. Where idle time is unknown (not macOS), the owner counts as at the computer unless the switch is on, replacing 'every prompt goes to Signal first'. Files: signal_cc/domain/routing.py, signal_cc/domain/texts.py, signal_cc/app/desk.py, signal_cc/ports.py, signal_cc/adapters/macos.py, signal_cc/adapters/files.py, signal_cc/entry/hooks.py, signal_cc/entry/wiring.py, tests/test_domain.py, tests/test_app.py, tests/test_adapters.py, README.md. Outside: a slash command at the Mac; a timer that turns the switch off.
acceptance: Given the switch is off and the Mac had input 5 s ago, when the owner sends 'away' on Signal, then the desk confirms and the next permission prompt goes to Signal.
Given the switch is on, when the Mac sees input while a prompt waits on Signal, then the prompt stays on Signal (no back-at-the-Mac hand-back).
Given the switch is on, when the owner sends 'back' or types a prompt at the Mac, then the switch is off and idle time decides again.
Given idle time is unknown, when a permission prompt arrives with the switch off, then nothing is sent to Signal; with the switch on, it goes to Signal.
Given a reply 'away' that quotes a waiting prompt, when it arrives, then it is read as that prompt's answer, not as a command.
Given the owner sends 'status', when the desk answers, then the answer says whether the switch is on.
why: G-2 follow-up; lands after land-status-ci; leave-digest waits on it because the digest fires when the owner leaves.
